Flexipede

A bio-inspired, modular myriapod robot for rough-terrain traversal — a single-actuator bipedal walking mechanism per module, plus a servo-driven active-yaw connector, scaled and validated from 1 to 6 modules across flat, rough, and stepped terrain.

S. J. Saha, Md. Abid Chowdhury, S. Islam, S. A. Deowan, S. E. Arman, A. K. Ghosh — Department of Robotics & Mechatronics Engineering, University of Dhaka

OVERVIEW

One motor, two legs, six segments.

Most myriapod-inspired robots lean on actuator-dense modules — up to four motors per segment — to coordinate a many-legged gait. Flexipede inverts that trade: each module walks on a single DC motor driving a mirrored four-bar linkage, with a second, independent servo handling only inter-module yaw. Complexity moves from the control stack into the mechanism itself.

The result is a fully 3D-printed, screw-assembled platform that was scaled from one to six modules and benchmarked across flat ground, stochastic rough terrain, and a stair rig — with the first reported Cost of Transport (CoT) figures for a robot in this class.

Abstract — Verbatim, CC BY 4.0

Rough-terrain exploration is critical for applications ranging from post-disaster search-and-rescue to planetary exploration. While conventional wheeled or bipedal robots often struggle in these environments, biological organisms like myriapods demonstrate superior adaptability. Inspired by this, we present Flexipede — a compact, modular robotic system that employs a hybrid actuation architecture, wherein each module integrates a single actuator for propulsive gait generation and a secondary actuator to enable distributed yaw control. Analytical kinematic modeling was employed to optimize linkage trajectories, with experimental results validating the system across six modular configurations and three distinct environments. The platform achieved locomotion speeds up to 9 cm/s and navigated obstacles up to 32 mm high, while linkage path deviations remained functionally negligible (mean deviation of 3.24%). Across all terrains, the system maintained a competitive average Cost of Transport (CoT) of 18.01.

HARDWARE DESIGN

The walking mechanism

A single DC motor drives a mirrored planar four-bar linkage per module — the coupler link's extended leg segment (L₂ext) traces a closed, forward-biased footpath, derived from loop-closure kinematics rather than tuned by hand.

Figure 1 — Kinematic model & gait simulation

(a) Four-bar linkage schematic with ground-reaction force decomposition. (b) Simulated closed-loop foot trajectory of the L₂ext tip. (c) Displacement, velocity and acceleration profiles over one gait cycle — bounded magnitudes confirm mechanical feasibility.

Bipedal module + active-yaw coupling

Two mirrored linkages share a common drive shaft (180° phase offset) to form a bipedal module. Between modules, a servo-driven spur gear meshes with a partial gear on the neighboring chassis, giving each joint independently commanded yaw — this is what lets a chain of modules steer as a coordinated body rather than a rigid train.

A closed-form turning-radius model (Eq. 11) was derived from this coupling geometry and used to predict, then validate, the minimum collision-free turning radius for every module count tested.

Figure 2 — CAD & modular assembly

(a) Mirrored 4-bar linkage on the shared drive shaft. (b) Servo-driven inter-module yaw coupling with retaining clip and hard stops. (c) Turning-radius geometry. (d) Three-module assembly, internal view.

Locomotion vs. modularity

Velocity and power draw across module counts (1–6), on flat, rough, and stepped terrain — five trials per point, 95% CI shaded.

Figure 5 — Velocity & power scaling

(d) Velocity peaks at n=5 on flat ground (9.30 ± 0.88 cm/s), and at n=4 on rough terrain / stairs. (e) Power draw scales with modularity on every surface, peaking during stair ascent (25.63 W at n=6).

FLAT

9.30 ± 0.88 cm/s

Peak at n = 5. Non-monotonic — dips between n=1 and n=2 before scaling up.

ROUGH

Obstacle clearance & postural stability

Maximum discrete-obstacle height cleared on the rough-terrain bed, plus chassis tilt angle (θ) during traversal, both as a function of module count (n = 3–6).

Figure 7 — Obstacle clearance

(a) Max cleared height falls monotonically: 33→30→28→20 mm for n=3→6. (c) n=5 has the lowest velocity variance; n=4 is the most energy-efficient (214.8 J/m).

Figure 8 — Postural stability

(a,b) Chassis tilt is symmetric and near-Gaussian for every configuration. (c) n=5 has the tightest tilt envelope (σθ = 5.17°); n=6 the widest (σθ = 11.30°) — stability does not scale monotonically.

Cost of Transport

CoT = P ⁄ (mgv), normalized for mass and speed — the standard metric for comparing legged-locomotion efficiency (Eq. 12).

Flat
Peaks at n=2 (41.74 ± 4.21); minimum at n=5 (17.73 ± 1.34); small uptick at n=6 (21.00 ± 0.89).
Rough
Stays low and stable — 15.94 (n=3) → 20.11 (n=6). Average across the terrain: 18.01.
Stairs
Highest CoT of all terrains beyond n=3; best at n=5 (36.98 ± 1.26), worst at n=6 (44.13 ± 2.08).
Benchmark
Rough-terrain CoT (18.01) is comparable to RHex (CoT ≈ 20) — notable for a robot this small.

01

Single-actuator bipedal linkage

A closed-form, kinematically-derived four-bar leg mechanism plus a servo-driven reconfigurable yaw connector.

02

Analytical model, physically validated

Loop-closure gait model and turning-radius model both checked directly against hardware trials.

03

Widest scaling study in its class

Six distinct module counts (1–6) across three terrain types — the most extensive scaling reported for this robot architecture.

04

First CoT benchmark for myriapod robots

None of the prior platforms surveyed report Cost of Transport; this establishes the first reference point (18.01, rough terrain).

LIMITATIONS & NEXT

Current limitations

  • ControlOpen-loop; no active stall recovery
  • CouplingOccasional gear slip under high torque
  • TerrainNo active inter-module pitch control (inclines)
  • PowerTested on external supply; onboard battery adds ~6–21% penalty (Appx. A)

Planned next steps

  • ControlClosed-loop, onboard odometry
  • MechanismActive inter-module pitch + refined yaw
  • KinematicsMathematically-optimized linkage dimensions
  • AutonomyAdaptive gait modulation, RL-based control
